shape.name: Shape F - Productive Skills (Traditional)
shape.description: Traditional productive skills lesson with preparation stages followed by speaking or writing output.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Here the focus is on helping learners practice their speaking or writing skills. The lesson can usually be divided into preparation for speaking/writing and speaking/writing task stages.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to [speak/write] about [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to draft a complete for-and-against essay from their plan, using key phrases for listing, adding, and contrasting, and then review and edit their draft.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
09-08-26
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
F (Productive Skills - Writing)
Materials:
Textbook writing workshop pp. 134-137, slideshow, essay topic cards, essay plans
Assessment:
Drafted and edited essay
Skills:
Writing

stages.stage_aim: To reactivate lessons 1 and 2 and set the theme: today we write the full essay from our plan
procedure: Show the splash slide. Ask: "What do you see? Someone writing a draft. What might this lesson be about?" Let students guess.
Advance to the title slide: "Write your essay." Confirm the theme: today we write the full for/against essay from our plan.
Show the "Why is this lesson important?" slide and read the bullets aloud.
Pairs recap: "What is your position? What are your three strongest ideas?" Students restate them.
Point to the Opinion-Reason-Evidence line at the bottom of the slide.

stages.stage_aim: To teach the hook-and-question introduction and draft the opening paragraph
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "The introduction."
Teach the strategy table: ask a question in the first line to hook the reader.
Reveal the Exercise 1 answers: the model asks "How do you listen to music?" and "So what are the advantages and disadvantages of doing this?" and mentions the alternative: downloads.
Exercise 2: students write their own introduction. 5 minutes (timer).

stages.stage_aim: To teach the key phrases for listing and adding ideas and find them in the model
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Key phrases."
Present the key phrases: listing (First, Second, Finally, Last but not least) and adding (What's more, On top of this, As well as, There's also the fact that).
Reveal the Exercise 3 gap-fill answers row by row.
Reveal the Exercise 4 answers: which phrases list ideas and which add information in the model essay.

stages.stage_aim: To teach the contrast words and apply them (Exercise 6)
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Make a contrast."
Present the contrast words: although, even if, even though, while.
Run the demo: "I like streaming, even though I still prefer downloads."
Reveal the Exercise 6 answers row by row.

stages.stage_aim: To teach attitude adverbs and match them to their meanings (Exercise 7)
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Use attitude adverbs."
Teach the strategy: one or two words make a point clear.
Reveal the Exercise 7 answers row by row. The four adverbs used in the model are obviously, increasingly, personally, and most importantly.

stages.stage_aim: For students to draft the two main paragraphs with key phrases and an attitude adverb (Exercise 8)
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Your main paragraphs."
Present the paragraph openers: advantages (Let's start by looking at the advantages) and disadvantages (Turning to the disadvantages).
Exercise 8: students write their two main paragraphs from their notes. 8 minutes (timer).
Monitor: key phrases and an attitude adverb appear in both paragraphs.

stages.stage_aim: To teach the conclusion strategies and key phrases and draft the final paragraph (Exercises 9 and 10)
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Write your conclusion."
Teach the strategy: repeat your opinion clearly, and show one point from the other side first.
Present the conclusion key phrases: To sum up, In conclusion, All in all, Overall, All things considered.
Reveal the Exercise 9 answer: the model uses "All things considered" and "overall".
Exercise 10: students write their conclusion. 5 minutes (timer).

stages.stage_aim: For students to revise their draft: pronouns, adverbs of degree, and cuts (page 137)
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Review and edit."
Teach the repetition strategy: use pronouns instead of repeating words. Reveal the Exercise 1 answers row by row.
Present the adverbs of degree and reveal the Exercise 3 answers.
Teach the cuts strategy: remove extra words.
Students complete the review exercises: check paragraphs, replace repeated words, add adverbs of degree, make cuts, and proofread. 8 minutes (timer).

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate the completed draft and set the final-copy task
procedure: Show the wrap-up slide: "Your essay is ready."
Students write the corrected final copy for homework.
Collect the drafts.

shape.note: For middle schoolers interested in SCR approach to productive skills, see Shape J instead.

metadata.topic: For and against essays: draft, link, and review
materials: Oxford Discover Futures 2, Unit "Writing workshop: A for and against essay", pp. 134–137
Slideshow — Lesson 3: Draft, Link, and Review
Essay topic cards — each student's assigned topic
Essay plans — each student's notes from Lesson 2
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to draft a complete for-and-against essay from their plan, using key phrases for listing, adding, and contrasting, and then review and edit their draft.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Learners will also be better able to use attitude adverbs to make their points clear and pronouns to avoid repetition.
answer_key: The model asks "How do you listen to music?" and "So what are the advantages and disadvantages of doing this?" The alternative mentioned is downloads: the writer says to forget downloads and just listen to music on streaming services.
1 Second. 2 What's more. 3 On top of this. 4 Last but not least.

Listing phrases: First, and most importantly; Second; Finally; first of all; Furthermore; Last but not least. Adding phrases: what's more; On top of this; As well as; There's also the fact that; another argument against them is.

1 "... while the free service with ads might seem fine at first, obviously they can get very annoying." 2 "... the audio quality is quite poor, although not everyone notices this." 3 "... even though I like the convenience of streaming, to me, it's much better to own the music."

1 obviously (everyone knows this), 2 basically (in a clear and simple way), 3 incredibly (really difficult to believe), 4 apparently (heard it, not sure it is true), 5 increasingly (more and more), 6 actually (in fact, it is true), 7 personally (this is my own opinion), 8 most importantly (more important than anything before). The four used in the model are obviously, increasingly, personally, and most importantly.
The model conclusion uses "All things considered" and "overall", with the contrast word "even though" before the opinion.

1 this refers to streaming music and forgetting downloads. 2 them refers to your playlists. 3 these refers to good Wi-Fi and a big data allowance. 4 which refers to the chance to stream music for free. 5 they refers to the ads. 6 this refers to the poor audio quality. 7 it refers to the music.

1 quite poor describes audio quality. 2 fairly big describes the data allowance. 3 pretty expensive describes streaming services. 4 very annoying describes the ads. 5 incredibly big describes the choice.
